name: Jet lag disorder
aliases: circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder, jet lag type

reference.source: Auerbach's Wilderness Medicine / Bove and Davis' Diving Medicine
clinicalPearls: A circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder that follows rapid travel across several time zones, when the internal body clock is misaligned with the destination's local time
Typical features are difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, daytime sleepiness, impaired daytime function, fatigue, and gastrointestinal upset
Eastward travel, which requires advancing the body clock, is generally harder to adjust to than westward travel
Severity broadly increases with the number of time zones crossed and tends to improve as the internal clock realigns over subsequent days
Management uses appropriately timed light exposure and avoidance, timed melatonin, and good sleep hygiene to shift the circadian clock in the desired direction
Strategic napping, adjusting meal and activity timing, and judicious caffeine use can support daytime alertness
It is self-limiting, resolving as the circadian system entrains to the new time zone
reference.pathophysiology: Jet lag disorder results from a temporary mismatch between the endogenous circadian clock, governed by the hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nucleus, and the external light-dark cycle at the destination after rapid transmeridian travel. The internal clock realigns only gradually, at a limited number of hours per day, so sleep-wake timing, alertness, hormone secretion such as melatonin, and gastrointestinal rhythms remain desynchronised until entrainment is complete. Because the clock naturally runs slightly longer than a day, delaying it (westward travel) is usually easier than advancing it (eastward travel).
additionalDifferentials: Other circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders (e.g. shift work disorder)
Effects of alcohol, caffeine, or medication on sleep
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from history of recent transmeridian travel and characteristic symptoms
Sleep diary documenting sleep-wake timing before and after travel
Assessment for coexisting sleep disorders where symptoms are prolonged
Screening for mood disorder if sleep disturbance persists
Actigraphy in selected or research settings to characterise the sleep-wake pattern
redFlags: Symptoms persisting well beyond the expected adjustment period, suggesting another sleep disorder
Excessive daytime sleepiness causing safety risk (e.g. while driving)
Features of obstructive sleep apnoea such as loud snoring and witnessed apnoeas
Significant mood disturbance accompanying the sleep problem
reference.prognosis: Jet lag is self-limiting and resolves as the circadian clock entrains to the new time zone, typically over several days depending on the number of time zones crossed and direction of travel; well-timed light and melatonin can shorten the adjustment.
pitfalls: Timing light exposure incorrectly and inadvertently shifting the clock the wrong way
Taking melatonin at the wrong time relative to the desired shift
Attributing persistent symptoms to jet lag rather than an underlying sleep disorder
Overusing alcohol or hypnotics, which can fragment sleep and delay adaptation
management: Use appropriately timed bright-light exposure and light avoidance to shift the circadian clock in the required direction, advancing it for eastward and delaying it for westward travel
Take timed melatonin around the destination bedtime to accelerate re-entrainment
Reinforce sleep hygiene and begin pre-flight gradual adjustment of sleep and meal timing towards the destination clock
Use strategic short naps and judicious daytime caffeine to support alertness while avoiding late-day stimulants
Offer a short course of a hypnotic for disabling insomnia during the adjustment period
Reassure that the disorder is self-limiting and resolves as the clock entrains over successive days
Reassess for a coexisting primary sleep or mood disorder if symptoms persist well beyond expected adjustment
